criteria.criterion: The note separates agent slots (model work) from build slots (cargo runs limited by disk and CPU), with a queue for build slots and its ordering and timeout behaviour described.
criteria.evidence: Section 3 compares the two slot kinds in a table: what each admits, how long it is held, what limits it, its count, and its config field. Section 4 describes the build-slot queue: a lock-file semaphore; strict priority classes (landing rebuild, then candidate checks, then producer commands), first in first out within a class, with ageing via build_age_promote_s; and a build_wait_s timeout with defined behaviour for checks (held, not failed), producer commands (exit 75) and the rebuild (no timeout).

criteria.criterion: The note proposes a shared compiled-output scheme (for example shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR, sccache or a warm baseline copy) with a disk-per-build estimate that is labeled as measured or estimate, and records the buy-first call on existing tools.
criteria.evidence: Section 5.2 compares options A to E: a shared target directory, sccache, a warm baseline copy, slot-owned warm directories, and smaller debug output. It chooses D with E. Section 5.3 gives 'Disk per build slot (estimate): 5 to 6 GB' and says plainly that no measurement backs it. A paragraph headed 'Buy-first call' records that Cargo profile settings and the existing sccache support come first and that custom caching is built only if those fall short.

criteria.criterion: The note covers the local landing-and-rebuild step, citing the status --snapshot output or code (crates/athena-core/src/status.rs) that shows it as the longest stage, and proposes how to shorten it.
criteria.evidence: Section 6.1 cites the 1069.2 min median (confirmed in the status output) and status.rs: landing_record_time at line 795 with .max() at line 806, landing_end at 811, landed_jobs at 876 with minutes_between at 895 (all confirmed by grep). It shows b4f5 listed in 19 landing records (confirmed: 19 files) and compares time to the first record with time to the newest. Section 6.2 proposes how to shorten the stage: measure it at the first record, record the rebuild duration R, batch the rebuild, and give the rebuild class-1 priority for a build slot.

criteria.criterion: The note gives numbers for how many agents and how many builds this machine can run at once, derived from 4 CPUs, 15 GB memory, ~27 GB free disk and 10-12 GB per build, with the arithmetic shown.
criteria.evidence: Section 7.1 shows the build arithmetic: (27-10)/12 = 1 build today, the existing disk formula giving 0 extra jobs, and 17/6 or 17/5 giving 2 to 3 slots by disk, capped at 2 by CPU. Section 7.2 shows the agent arithmetic: (15-1.5-6)/0.5 = 15, a pessimistic case of 9 and an optimistic case of 25, plus disk and CPU checks. The answer is 12 agent slots, rising to 16 after measurement, and 2 builds. Memory and CPU figures are labeled estimates.

criteria.criterion: The note lists the build order as small numbered changes, each landable on its own; each names the crates/ files it touches and how its effect will be measured (a named metric and where it is read).

findings.summary: The slot-directory scheme cleans workspace-crate output after every command, so a producer would rebuild the workspace crates on every cargo command
findings.evidence: Step 2 links the slot directory into the job 'for the duration of one command'. Step 3 runs `cargo clean -p <each workspace member>` 'when the command ends'. A producer typically runs cargo build or test many times. Under this scheme each run recompiles every workspace crate, whereas today it gets an incremental rebuild in its own target directory. The note weighs only the per-job rebuild. A simpler alternative: keep the slot bound to the job for all of the producer's commands, or clean only when the job releases the slot. Build job 5 measures only the second build's wall time. The note also admits it did not read env.rs to see whether the build-directory check resolves symlinks, so whether the D46 isolation rule still holds is unconfirmed.
